research_theme: Model scaling and factuality / hallucination evaluation
research_question: Does increasing model size reliably improve factuality or hallucination evaluation?
focal_claim_text: On FACTBENCH, Llama3.1-405B-Instruct performs comparably to or worse than Llama3.1-70B-Instruct across reported tiers.
comparison_claim_text: Most evaluated hallucination metrics do not show consistent improvement as model parameter count increases; GPT-4 is the only metric reported to consistently reject the no-scaling-effect null hypothesis in the tested analyses.
adjudication_rationale: The two findings concern different sides of the model-evaluation relationship. P006 compares the factual precision of Llama 3.1 405B and 70B on FACTBENCH using VERIFY and baseline evaluators; VERIFY scores are lower for 405B at Hard, Moderate and Easy tiers, while FactCheck-GPT is slightly higher for 405B on Hard and Moderate. P007 examines whether hallucination-detection metrics themselves improve as the size of the evaluated language models increases, using TruthfulQA and FaithDial for its scaling analysis. P007 reports inconsistent metric trends and says only GPT-4 consistently rejects the no-scaling-effect null in those tested analyses. A model's factuality score and a metric's sensitivity to model scaling are distinct constructs. The results are related but do not directly contradict or validate one another.
source_verification: P006: PDF p.6, Table 1; PDF p.7, Table 2 and §7.1. P007: PDF p.4, Finding 4 and Table 2; PDF p.6, Limitations (scaling findings limited to TruthfulQA and FaithDial).
decision_note: Do not interpret P007 as a general claim that all larger LLMs are less factual. It evaluates metric trends on specified datasets, not a direct controlled comparison of the same 70B/405B models in P006.

research_theme: Prompt difficulty, entity familiarity and hallucination
research_question: Do harder or less familiar factual prompts increase hallucination risk?
focal_claim_text: For Llama 2-Chat (7B), hallucination rates rise as queried entity frequency in pretraining knowledge decreases.
comparison_claim_text: Across evaluated models, FACTBENCH factual precision is lower on Hard prompts than Moderate and Easy prompts.
adjudication_rationale: P005 reports a long-tail pattern between Wikipedia entity frequency and Llama 2-Chat (7B) hallucination rates: hallucinations are lower for the most frequent entities and higher for entities in the long tail. P006 reports that factual precision on FACTBENCH declines as prompt difficulty moves from Easy to Moderate to Hard. Both findings indicate that factual performance depends on what the model is asked, but they operationalize difficulty differently. Entity frequency is a proxy for familiarity with pretraining knowledge, whereas FACTBENCH tiers are benchmark prompt-difficulty categories. This provides useful context for interpreting prompt difficulty as a factor in factuality, but it does not establish that entity frequency causes the FACTBENCH tier effect.
source_verification: P005: PDF p.5, Figure 1(b) and §5.1 Familiarity of Pre-training Knowledge. P006: PDF p.6, Table 1 and PDF p.7, Table 2; factual precision falls from Easy to Moderate to Hard across listed models.
decision_note: P005's frequency analysis is observational and specific to Llama 2-Chat (7B) and its constructed entity-query set. Avoid causal language.

research_theme: Scientific QA benchmarks measure different grounding capabilities
research_question: How demanding is scientific document-grounded QA and evidence tracing?
focal_claim_text: On CLAIM-BENCH, the best reported claim-identification F1 is 0.59 (Claude 3.5), while the best evidence-extraction F1 is 0.47 (GPT-4-Turbo).
comparison_claim_text: LitTraceQA contains 4,978 unique questions grounded in 4,859 unique gold papers through 8,612 paper-question links.
adjudication_rationale: CLAIM-BENCH evaluates claim identification and evidence extraction from AI research papers, reporting best claim-identification F1 of 0.59 and best evidence-extraction F1 of 0.47 in its tested models and strategies. LitTraceQA is a broader traceable scientific-QA benchmark organized around three stages: retrieval of relevant papers, grounding in typed evidence (including tables, figures, text, equations/algorithms and citation context), and answer generation. Its collection statistics describe benchmark scale and evidence diversity, not a comparable model F1 result. The benchmarks address related scientific grounding problems, but they evaluate different task contracts and performance dimensions.
source_verification: P008: PDF p.7, Table 2 and §5.3. P011: PDF p.6, Table 1/Figure 2; PDF pp.7–9, evaluation protocol and corpus analysis.
decision_note: Do not compare CLAIM-BENCH F1 values with LitTraceQA collection counts. One is model extraction performance; the other is dataset composition and a staged evaluation contract.

research_theme: Scientific QA benchmarks measure different grounding capabilities
research_question: How demanding is scientific document-grounded QA and evidence tracing?
focal_claim_text: On CLAIM-BENCH, the best reported claim-identification F1 is 0.59 (Claude 3.5), while the best evidence-extraction F1 is 0.47 (GPT-4-Turbo).
comparison_claim_text: All memory-only challengers were wrong on 3,080 LitTraceQA questions (61.9%) during benchmark construction; this is not a retrieval-augmented evaluation result.
adjudication_rationale: CLAIM-BENCH measures how well models identify claims and retrieve their supporting evidence from AI papers. LitTraceQA's 61.9% figure means that all closed-book challenger models failed on 3,080 of 4,978 questions during benchmark construction. This is a construction-time hardness filter intended to reduce questions answerable from model memory alone; it is not a retrieval-augmented system score. The result contextualizes why evidence-grounded scientific QA needs explicit paper access, but it cannot be treated as a comparable success or failure rate against CLAIM-BENCH's claim/evidence F1 scores.
source_verification: P008: PDF p.7, Table 2 and §5.3. P011: PDF p.6, Table 1/Figure 2; PDF p.8, dataset construction and hardness explanation; PDF p.9, corpus analysis explicitly distinguishes hardness labels from RAG leaderboard results.
decision_note: Preserve the denominator: 3,080/4,978 = 61.9%. It is not a RAG baseline performance result.

research_theme: Scientific QA benchmarks measure different grounding capabilities
research_question: How demanding is scientific document-grounded QA and evidence tracing?
focal_claim_text: On CLAIM-BENCH, the best reported claim-identification F1 is 0.59 (Claude 3.5), while the best evidence-extraction F1 is 0.47 (GPT-4-Turbo).
comparison_claim_text: In QASPER, 55.5% of questions require evidence from multiple paragraphs, and 13% require evidence from tables or figures.
adjudication_rationale: CLAIM-BENCH tests extraction of claims and associated evidence from AI research papers, with the best reported F1 values of 0.59 for claim identification and 0.47 for evidence extraction. QASPER measures information-seeking question answering over full NLP papers; 55.5% of questions require evidence from multiple paragraphs and 13% require tables or figures. QASPER therefore adds context about the complexity and diversity of evidence needed for scientific-paper understanding. However, the tasks differ: claim/evidence extraction is not the same as answering reader questions, and the metrics cannot be compared directly.

decision_note: QASPER's 13% table/figure statistic describes question evidence requirements; do not imply CLAIM-BENCH has the same evidence distribution.
